episode_title: Six More Stories That Should Be Films

stories.summary: Amit retells a thought experiment from Deepak VS, whom he had recently interviewed on The Seen and the Unseen: replace the IIT entrance exam with a swimming test. Deepak argued the engineers would be just as good. Amit got carried away and said they would be better, since the exam really selects for hunger, passion and initiative. Deepak corrected him: by the second year the system would be gamed again, with Kota running swimming classes and billboards of coaches in Speedos. Amit builds a film on this. A boy who genuinely loves engineering is stuck on a treadmill of IIT-sized pools. He is beaten by kids who don't care about engineering, and the person he is falling for hits him from the next lane to get ahead. He escapes to the open sea, where he finally loves swimming, the fishermen and the sea creatures. His coaching grades collapse, he fails, and his mother stops talking to him. He swims out past the danger marker into a storm and disappears.
stories.insight: Any test for a deeper quality soon gets gamed until it measures only itself. The real joy of learning lies outside the lane, but the system rewards only racing from this point to that point.
stories.quote: So one day he goes to the nearby seaside and he says, You know, to hell with the swimming pool. Why should I stay in my lane?

stories.topic: The Lost Plutonium of Nanda Devi
stories.summary: In the 1950s China was building nuclear weapons, and spy satellites could not yet watch the Tibetan plateau. The CIA approached India with a plan. An Indian Army team had just climbed Kanchenjunga, so the idea was to put a permanent listening station on its summit, at around 28,000 feet, looking down on Tibet. It would be powered by a plutonium battery that would run for years. The Indian climbers flatly refused: no one could carry a 70 kg battery up Kanchenjunga. They proposed Nanda Devi instead. The CIA quietly recruited elite American climbers, swearing them to secrecy with all expenses paid. On the second attempt a storm hit, so the team lashed the equipment to rocks at a memorised spot (there was no GPS) and retreated. When they returned, the place was unrecognisable and the device was gone. It was never found. One theory is that the Chinese climbed up from their side and took it. Another is that the always-warm plutonium melted its way hundreds of metres into the glacier. If it ever reaches the Ganga, tens of millions could die. India's cover story was that hikers and hippies were damaging a precious reserve, so Nanda Devi was shut and searched with Geiger counters for years.
stories.insight: Real history can be stranger than any pitch room would allow. Ajay notes that a Cold War spy plan and an environmental closure turn out to be the same story, and the danger is still up there, with a half-life of thousands of years.
stories.quote: Now, the amount of plutonium in that battery, if it found its way down the melting glacier ultimately into the Ganga, then tens of millions of people in the Gangetic Plain would die.

stories.topic: The Soviet Guard Who Held Plutonium in the Snow
stories.summary: During the Soviet atom bomb project, NKVD jailers under Beria watched over physicists they did not trust. The guards had orders to shoot all the physicists if the first test failed. One guard burst in on a physicist holding a piece of metal and accused him of being a malingerer passing off stainless steel as plutonium. The physicist remembered that plutonium is always warm from radioactive decay. He told the guard to hold it outside at minus twenty degrees. The guard stood out for half an hour and got frostbite on his earlobes, but the metal stayed warm.
stories.insight: A neat piece of physics, the constant warmth of radioactive decay, appears here as a survival tactic under terror. In Stalin's system, winning the argument only bought you a day.
stories.quote: The guard went outside, stood in the freezing cold for half an hour. Everything else in his body froze. His lobes got frostbite, but the plutonium stayed warm. And then he came back and said, Okay, fine, then I'll kill you tomorrow.

stories.topic: Delhi College and a City in Churn (1803–1857)
stories.summary: Drawing on Swapna Liddle's The Broken Script, Amit pitches a web series set in Delhi between the East India Company's win in the second Anglo-Maratha war (1803) and 1857. The Mughals rule in name while the Company holds real power. Princes scheme against each other, and Bahadur Shah Zafar was a plotter, not the weak poet of popular depiction. Persian, the language of power, vanishes in fifty years. Printing presses arrive, and newspapers and poetry flourish. At the centre is Delhi College. Its endowment came from one Fazal Ali on the condition that teaching be in local languages, so Western knowledge ended up being taught in Hindustani, which had no technical terms for it. The cast includes Ghalib, a cultural legend who was also dodging moneylenders and flattering the British, and Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who wrote obsequiously as a Mughal emperor's emissary. 1857 ends it all. The British see the revolt as Muslim-led and deepen a Hindu-Muslim divide. The college dissolves into nothingness.
stories.insight: Early 19th-century Delhi was a living experiment in colliding worlds: language, knowledge, print and politics all changing at once. It was ended by violence rather than by its own failure.
stories.quote: It seems to me to be a great locus of all this, because you have the collision of the worlds there.

stories.summary: Ramchandra, born in 1821 and a teacher at Delhi College, tried to explain the rules of calculus using algebra in a treatise on maxima and minima. It reached the British mathematician Augustus De Morgan, who was blown away and tried hard to promote him. Someone later called the pair the Hardy and Ramanujan of their age, except that Hardy succeeded and De Morgan couldn't. Ramchandra was also a fearless rationalist who attacked traditional medicine and every religion, local and Western. He started journal after journal to be a public intellectual. Then, around thirty, in 1852, he converted to Christianity, which nothing in his writing explains. After 1857 he became headmaster of some random school.
stories.insight: Genius alone doesn't decide who becomes famous. Patronage and historical rupture do too. People also remain mysteries; we can't fully explain even well-documented lives.
stories.quote: Ramchandra is a mathematician born in 1821 who tries to explain the rules of calculus using algebra.

stories.topic: Sayyid Ahmad Khan Goes Back to School at Thirty
stories.summary: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, who founded Aligarh Muslim University, was taught by private tutors until about twenty, then went out and made a name for himself. At thirty, which was middle-aged given life expectancy then, he decided he didn't know enough. He hired six private tutors for six subjects and educated himself all over again.
stories.insight: It takes real humility for an accomplished person to admit their gaps and start learning again. That is the mark of a serious mind.
stories.quote: At the age of thirty, he decides I don't know enough. Right? An accomplished man having the humility to say this, I don't know enough.

stories.summary: In this period, the star attraction that every Delhi newspaper needed was not gossip but poetry. The Delhi Urdu Akhbar carried news from Afghanistan, Herat, France, Russia, Gwalior, Nagpur and more, and in 1841 ran an editorial arguing for widow remarriage. Mushairas were everywhere, and their verses were printed as tazkiras that sold so well that one Karimuddin, who didn't care for poetry, began holding regular mushairas just so he could publish them. Another tazkira opened with essays teaching readers about meter and metaphor.
stories.insight: A mass audience once paid for verse and serious debate. What a public consumes is not fixed. Even commercial greed can end up funding a cultural scene.
stories.quote: Poets, in a sense, were the great public figures of their time.

stories.topic: The German Navy Scuttles Itself at Scapa Flow
stories.summary: Germany built a navy to challenge the Royal Navy, but it was not ready when the First World War began in 1914. Its shiny new ships, about half the size of the British fleet, mostly sat out the war in dock. The Treaty of Versailles capped the German army at 100,000 men, allowed no tanks and no navy, and ordered the fleet handed to Britain at Scapa Flow in the far north of Scotland. That meant more than a hundred ships and more than a hundred submarines. During the handover the German sailors were treated pettily, without enough food or sanitation. Instead of surrendering, they had mounted explosives, and some seventy or eighty warships blew up and sank one by one. Many died because evacuations weren't planned.
stories.insight: Treaties are signed by governments but carried out by people, and people can refuse. Amit raises the hard question: a soldier should obey orders, yet we would cheer the same defiance had the sides been reversed.
stories.quote: You may have signed the treaty of Versailles. We refuse. We're not giving you the ships.

stories.summary: Since the first nuclear tests, radioactive dust has spread everywhere, contaminating iron ore, coal and steel mills. Geiger counters need steel that isn't radioactive to begin with, or they lose their discriminating power. The source of clean, pre-bomb steel is the scuttled German fleet. Divers cut pieces off the wrecks at Scapa Flow and bring them up. The Geiger counters used to hunt for the Nanda Devi plutonium were made from this steel.
stories.insight: Seemingly separate stories, a scuttled fleet in Scotland and lost plutonium in the Himalayas, turn out to be physically linked. As Amit observes, the ships became more useful underwater than they ever were afloat.
stories.quote: Where do you find steel that is untarnished by nuclear bombs? The answer Scapa Flow.

stories.summary: Amit pitches a low-budget film told entirely through naturalistic vlogs, with no third-person camera. At a vloggers' meetup, cameras replace guns in a Mexican standoff. Each vlogger films themselves with others in the background, and the camera pulls back into a hall of mirrors. The heart of the film is love. A likable everyday-Joe vlogger falls for a new vlogger who seems completely constructed: beautiful, androgynous, impossible to read. Love shocks him in two ways. Someone else becomes real to him, and he must ask whether his love depends on the other person's genitals. The arc Amit wants is that this androgynous person turns out to be the one being true to themselves. Everyone else, including the hero in gentle ways, is performing.
stories.insight: Social media promises authenticity, but you can be sincere without knowing yourself. Sometimes the person who looks most artificial is the most honest one.
stories.quote: So it's just a beautiful, spectacular scene to satisfy the Tarantino in me, but nowhere near the crux of the story. The crux of the story always has to do with love.

stories.summary: In 1935 Mussolini, dreaming of a new Roman Empire, invaded what is now Ethiopia and Somalia. His soldiers were unwarlike men who mostly wanted a good time, and their hearts, and stomachs, weren't in the fight. Groups of soldiers in the boondocks rebelled over bad military food. The fix: sheep from Italy were loaded onto planes, strapped to parachutes and dropped one by one over the army camps. Live sheep rather than meat made sense because, with refrigeration limited, the live animal kept the meat fresh. At least one blurry black-and-white photo exists. Ajay offers it as a scene for writers to build a story around.
stories.insight: Armies march on their stomachs. A near-mutiny was averted by solving a food problem, and the solution was absurd but workable.
stories.quote: The sheep is a life support system. It has an immune system. It keeps the meat fresh.

recommendations.creator: Swapna Liddle
recommendations.context: The source of Amit's Delhi College story, covering Delhi from about 1803 to 1857.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the finest history books he has read in recent years and the best book of quasi-Mughal history he has come across. It brings alive the collapse of Persian, the print and poetry boom, Ramchandra, and the end of it all in 1857.

recommendations.item: Swapna Liddle and the Many Shades of Delhi (Episode 367, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit says he had never heard of Ramchandra until he did this episode and read the book.
recommendations.reason: A long-form conversation with the historian behind the Delhi College material, for anyone who wants more of this period.

recommendations.item: Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face (Episode 373, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The source of the IIT-by-swimming thought experiment that opens the episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Deepak, an entrepreneur in his mid-twenties, an incredibly fine thinker. It was Deepak who pointed out that any new entrance test would be gamed within a year.

recommendations.creator: Stevie Smith
recommendations.context: Read aloud in full to close the swimming story.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's favourite poems. It is about a man whose lifelong distress was mistaken for waving, which mirrors his drowning IIT aspirant.

recommendations.creator: Robert Beckhusen
recommendations.context: Cited during the Nanda Devi plutonium story.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a beautiful Wired article. It tells the American side, including how the CIA secretly recruited elite US climbers one by one.

recommendations.item: Hiking in the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve
recommendations.context: An aside while explaining the cover story used to close off Nanda Devi.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the world's most glorious hiking regions and tells listeners who have never hiked to 'run, not walk' there.

recommendations.reason: A recurring motif of that series was a person in a swimming pool. It is also the precedent for pitching a long-form web series, as Amit does for Delhi College.

recommendations.item: Five Epic Stories That Must Be Films (Episode 29, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The other earlier mixed-bag stories episode Amit mentions.
recommendations.reason: More stories in the same format.

core_ideas.explanation: An entrance exam is really a filter for hunger, passion and initiative, not for the subject itself. That is why even swimming might work in year one. But once a test becomes the gate, a coaching industry rebuilds itself around it, and the test stops measuring what you wanted.
core_ideas.quote: you see what will happen in the second year is that the system will get gamed again. You know? So Kota will start having swimming classes

core_ideas.concept: Reality Is Not Obliged to Be Reasonable
core_ideas.explanation: Fiction must be plausible, and reality doesn't have to be. Ajay's elevator pitch for Nanda Devi (CIA, China, plutonium, hippies, tens of millions dead in UP) sounds like word soup, yet every word is true. Non-fiction is often the richest source of stories.
core_ideas.quote: The difference between reality and fiction is that reality is not obliged to be reasonable.

core_ideas.explanation: In early 19th-century Delhi, Persian held the place English holds in India today: nobody's mother tongue, but the language of power and of every official document. Within fifty years it was gone, and parents' whole stock of learning became useless in front of their children. Amit contrasts this with today's supposedly unprecedented change: he still speaks the language he spoke as a child, under the same government and maps.
core_ideas.quote: if you are a kid who's ten years old, you look at your parents and they're completely helpless in the new world.

core_ideas.explanation: Before print, language evolves through a fluid, spontaneous order. When printing presses spread, writing a word down fixes it in one form and one usage. That brings stability but also loses much of the flux.
core_ideas.quote: When you write down a word, you ossify it.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge Needs a Language Ready to Carry It
core_ideas.explanation: Delhi College taught Western knowledge in Hindustani because its endower insisted on local languages. The British ignored the local knowledge systems, though, and the language had no technical terms for the new content. Amit notes this mismatch is a problem to this day.
core_ideas.quote: So it is a complete mismatch because Hindustani doesn't have the language or the ways of thinking to be able to communicate all of these things. There are no technical terms, nothing, a lot of which is a problem to this day.

core_ideas.concept: The Many Currents We Swim In
core_ideas.explanation: Ghalib was a legend who also ran from moneylenders and flattered the British. Ram Mohan Roy was a fearless reformer who also wrote obsequiously to a Mughal emperor. People are pulled at once by history, by society and by personal need, so no single act defines them.
core_ideas.quote: But you realize that there are different currents that we swim in at the same time. Some are the currents of history, some are the currents of society, and there's all this other personal stuff happening.

core_ideas.explanation: A soldier is supposed to follow orders, and if everyone rationalises disobedience, things fall apart. Yet our verdict on Scapa Flow depends on whose side we're on: had Britain lost and Nazis been taking its navy, we would cheer the sailors who blew it up. Ajay sets it beside Mers-el-Kébir. There French sailors chose to obey orders rather than join the British, who then opened fire and killed thousands.
core_ideas.quote: At a normative level, as a soldier, you should follow orders. Yes. That is the deal. We can say that I must follow my conscience or you know, et cetera, et cetera. But the point is if everyone starts rationalizing like that, you kinda get screwed.

core_ideas.explanation: Since nuclear testing began, nearly all newly made steel carries radioactive contamination, so sensitive Geiger counters need pre-bomb steel salvaged from the Scapa Flow wrecks. That links a 1919-era naval mutiny to a Cold War spy mission in the Himalayas. Seemingly separate histories are physically woven together.
core_ideas.quote: See, stories and stories are all coming together. Mers-el-Kébir and Nanda Devi and now Scapa Flow, all the story, the tapestry of the world brings everything together.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's definition: we are all lazy, so we can fake a persona only briefly, and the one self we can sustain without effort is our own. Online, audiences sense contrivance and performers tire of it. Amit adds that a pose you keep working at becomes yours, and the mask often becomes the face.
core_ideas.quote: There is only one person that I can be without effort, and that is me.

core_ideas.concept: Character Is a River, Not a Rock
core_ideas.explanation: Character is contingent. Skip breakfast and your brain chemistry, and your behaviour, shift by evening. We may be sincere yet not know ourselves, so a fixed, authentic self is harder to define than we assume.
core_ideas.quote: we think my character is a rock. No, it isn't. My character is a river.

core_ideas.concept: Love as Realising Someone Else Is Real
core_ideas.explanation: Using Iris Murdoch's line, Amit argues that we all live with main character syndrome, treating everyone else as a prop. Love shatters this by making another person undeniably real.
core_ideas.quote: We are all in the main character syndrome. We are all living this virtual reality in our heads where we are the main character, everyone else is a prop.

core_ideas.concept: Lust Is Honest, Love Can Be a Cover
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says he prefers lust to love because lust is what it is. 'Love' can be an evolutionary adaptation or a cover for wanting status, social acceptance or a certain companion. Science suggests we mostly act for reasons other than those we tell ourselves, and rationalise after the fact.
core_ideas.quote: most of what we do, we don't do it for the reasons we think we do it for. We are doing post facto rationalization

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay asks for a redemptive ending after the drowning story, and Amit replies: 'Redemption, you want a happy story. We all die.' Then Ajay delivers a tale of lost plutonium that could poison the Gangetic plain, and Amit retorts: 'This is your redemptive story.'

Amit proposes merchandise for their joint production: a T-shirt reading 'Okay, fine, I'll kill you tomorrow,' the Soviet guard's verdict after the plutonium proved itself. He calls it 'the best T-shirt line ever.'

Ajay pitches the Nanda Devi story to Amit as a movie mogul in two minutes: 'America, India, cooperation, CIA, intelligence, China, nuclear proliferation, plutonium... tens of millions of people in UP could die. Hippies at Nanda Devi.' He says Amit would call it 'word soup.'
Ajay: 'Gentle reader, you should tell your great great grandchildren don't live in the Gangetic plain.' Amit: 'Gentle reader don't have great great grandchildren.'
Ajay on Soviet vocabulary: 'You got to be a communist to know the phrase malingerer. It's used in Russian to basically kill people.'
Ajay sums up the Delhi College mismatch: 'It's like we're teaching the Magna Carta, but we're doing it in Urdu.'
Ajay on the Treaty of Versailles handover: 'You've got an Amazon delivery happening. Think of a delivery of a navy.'
Amit on the wrecks becoming Geiger-counter steel: 'in a perverse way, the ships were more useful under the water than they would have been over the water.'
Amit makes Ajay say 'vlogging' before starting his story: 'Well done. I'm proud of you. Many people can't do this. So already, achievement unlocked.'
Amit insists he won't give spoilers about how the vlogging film ends, then admits: 'But actually the truth is I haven't thought of that yet.'

Ajay voices the Italian soldiers in Ethiopia: 'Mamma Mia... I'll go out to far away countries and I'll kill strangers, but you gotta feed me.' When Amit asks why not drop boxes of meat, Ajay explains the sheep is 'a life support system,' and Amit adds that 'it can keep the soldiers company in other ways.'
Stevie Smith's 'Not Waving but Drowning' ('I was much too far out all my life, and not waving but drowning'), read as the coda to the IIT-swimmer story.
Iris Murdoch: 'Love is the extremely difficult realization that someone other than oneself is real,' used to frame the vlogger who falls in love.

The Mexican standoff ('I have a gun to your head, you have a gun to her head, she has a gun to my head,' as Ajay puts it), Reservoir Dogs and Tarantino, reimagined with vloggers pointing cameras instead of guns.

'A ship is safe in the harbor, but that's not what ships are for.' Ajay applies the saying to the German fleet that sat out the First World War in dock, and Amit chimes in with Otis Redding's 'Sittin' on the Dock of the Bay.'
Ramchandra and Augustus De Morgan were once called the Hardy and Ramanujan of their age, the difference being that Hardy succeeded in championing his protégé and De Morgan couldn't.
Bahadur Shah Zafar is usually shown in popular culture as a weak, ineffectual poet-king. Amit says Liddle's history shows a schemer and plotter who 'contained multitudes.'
Mers-el-Kébir in Algeria, an earlier episode's story where the British destroyed the French fleet, offered as the moral mirror to Scapa Flow.
Ajay's aside that, like the Kaiser's navy in 1914, Hitler in 1939 also moved before key pieces of his military build-out were ready.
Ajay contrasts the IIT-swimmer allegory with 'silly TV serials about children preparing in Kota.'
The sign-off: 'everything, my friends, is stories. Everything, my friends, is everything.'
